column2: The whole world goes joined with the ordinance of the end, and all beings go always on the road already travelled.
As sesame and mustard scented with a little flower do not give up their own smell, such is the seeing of the subtle.
The same, scented again and again with many flowers, gives up its own smell and stays with the flowers' scent.
So one joined with hundreds of births, among those attached to qualities, has the fault turned away by intellect, by effort born of practice.
Hear how, Danava, those who are attached and those detached by their own action gain the particulars of action.
And how they proceed and in what they stand, lord: that I shall explain in order; hear it here one-pointed.
The glorious Hari Narayana, the lord, without beginning or end, creates beings, the fixed and the moving.
He is in all beings both perishable and imperishable, of the nature of eleven modifications, drinking the world with his rays.
Know the earth as his feet, heaven as his head, the directions as his arms, Daitya, and space as his hearing.
The sun is made of his energy; the mind abides in the moon; intellect is ever in knowledge; taste goes on in the waters.
The planets are between his brows, best of the Danavas; the circle of stars is in his eyes, and the earth is in his feet.
Know rajas, tamas and sattva as of the nature of Narayana; he is the mouth of the stages, and the fruit of action, they say.
He is also the fruit of non-action, the supreme imperishable; the metres are his hair, and Sarasvati the syllable.
Of many supports, many mouths, he rests in the heart as dharma; he is Brahman, supreme dharma, austerity, and being and non-being.
Endowed with scripture and the grasp of the shastras, he is the sixteen priests and the sacrifice; he is the Grandfather and Vishnu; he is the Ashvins and Purandara.
Mitra, Varuna, Yama and the giver of wealth: those who see separately find oneness in him; know that this whole world is in the power of the one god.
Of the one who has become many, lord of the Daityas, this one speaks of his oneness; a creature sees by knowledge, and then sattva shines.
Creatures stand and roam in thousands of crores of dissolutions and emissions; of the measure of the creation of beings there are many thousands of ponds, Daitya.
Those ponds are a yojana wide, deep by a krosha and unfathomable; five hundred in length each; each is the extent of a yojana.
If one were to take water from a pond with the tip of a hair, once a day and not a second time, when they are emptied know one emission made, and likewise one dissolution of beings.
These are the classes of souls, the supreme measure: black, smoky, blue as its middle; red, more bearable, but happiness; turmeric-coloured, very happy; and white.
The supreme white, spotless, griefless, free of weariness, succeeds, lord of the Danavas; having gone through thousands of births in wombs, the soul reaches perfection.
The goal the god declared by sight, having gone, he declared the auspicious sight; the goal of beings is made by colour again, and colour is made by time, lord of asuras.
A hundred and fourteen thousand is the supreme goal of the quality of the soul; know the ascent made so, and their stations and exits.
The goal of the black colour is the lowest; he sinks in hell, being cooked, and in station; for the bad goals of his, they speak of very many emissions of beings.
Having roamed a hundred thousand, he afterward gains the green colour; and he, helpless, dwells in it, at the end of the age, his self covered with darkness.
When he is joined with the quality of goodness and strives with his own intellect, driving out darkness, he reaches the red colour; blue, he turns about in the human world.
There, afflicted by the bonds of his own deeds in dissolution and emission, after a hundred dissolutions and emissions have passed, he reaches the turmeric colour.
Of turmeric colour, he stays in thousands of emissions, roaming; unfreed, in hell, Daitya, then another ten thousand,
and five thousand goals of his, and the four made by the dissolution; know him as freed from hell and from all other births.
He sports constantly in the world of the gods; fallen from there, he comes to humanity; for eight hundred dissolutions and emissions, remaining among mortals, he attains immortality.
Then he falls from that by the working of time and stays on the black level; how this soul-world succeeds, I shall tell you, hero of the asuras.
Divine formations, seven hundred: red, turmeric, and likewise white; resorting to this white, he runs to the worlds that are lesser and most worthy.
Eight and sixty hundreds that are opposed to the minds of the greatly radiant; the supreme goal of the white colour is three, which are shut up, great-natured one.
One unwished dissolution and emission, and four others; he dwells without a master; of the colour in this state the supreme goal is of the perfected, the distinguished, free of weariness.
Without a master he dwells in the seventy among them, a hundred dissolutions and emissions with a remainder; returning from there to the human world, the great one comes to humanity.
Returning from there in order, he stays at the head of the creation of beings; seven times he goes to the worlds, his dwelling made by dissolution and emission.

Having reckoned seven dissolutions and floods, he stays in the world of the perfected; then he reaches the imperishable, endless seat of the god Vishnu, Brahma, Shesha and Nara, and of the supreme god Vishnu.
At the time of dissolution, with bodies burnt up, the subjects ever come to Brahma; and the gods all of active nature, and those immortals from the world of Brahma too.
The emission of subjects with the remaining time: souls go to their own places; at the end they go to the seat of the remainderless, men who are alike in all calamities.
Those who fall in order from the world of the perfected go the goal of those; the other souls, of their strength and shape, go to their own ordinance by reversal.
As long as one is enjoying the remainder, and in the white are subjects and the two gods, so long, then, in them, his state is pure; having restrained this form of the five senses,
he reaches that pure supreme goal, ever seeking with a pure mind; then he reaches the imperishable stable Brahman, hard to attain, eternal. Thus has Narayana's power been told you, undismayed one."
[Vritra said:] "That being so, I have no despondency; I see rightly what you say; hearing your words, undismayed one, I am today stainless and free of sin.

This is the wheel of the greatly radiant Vishnu, blessed great sage, unfollowed in valour, the endless, eternal seat in which all creations go on. He is the great-souled best of Persons; in him this whole world is established."
[Bhishma said:] Having spoken so, Kaunteya, Vritra gave up his breaths, and joining himself, reached the highest place.
[Yudhishthira said:] "Was this the blessed god Janardana, grandsire, whom Sanatkumara described to Vritra long ago?"
[Bhishma said:] "The blessed one stays at the root, by his own endless energy, and abiding there creates those states in many forms, great ascetic.
Know that Keshava Achyuta is a quarter and a half of him; the wise one sustains the three worlds with a quarter and a half.
He who stands on this side, the stable one, turns at the end of the aeon; the blessed mighty lord sleeps in the waters; the Creator, serene of soul, roams the eternal worlds.
The endless one makes everything not empty; Sanatkumara moves through the worlds; and the great-souled Aniruddha creates all this variegated world that rests in him."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Vritra, knower of the highest truth, saw, I think, the good goal of the self; therefore he is happy and does not grieve, grandsire.
The white, of white birth, the accomplished one does not return, sinless one, freed from the animal goal and from hell, grandsire.
One who stands in the turmeric or red colour, covered with tamasic deeds, would see an animal birth.
But we are greatly fallen into calamity, red, in a mouth of misery; what goal shall we reach, the blue or the lowest, the black?"
[Bhishma said:] "Pandavas, endowed with pure birth, of strict vows, having sported in the worlds of the gods, you will come to humanity again.

You will pass happily the emission of subjects in due time, enjoying pleasures among the gods, and you will happily go to the number of the perfected; let there be no fear for you; you are all stainless."
[Yudhishthira said:] "This, dear, is hard to know, of Vishnu of immeasurable radiance; how did he know that state, tiger among kings?
What you tell, Achyuta, I believe; but a further question has arisen in me from seeing the unmanifest.
How was Vritra slain by Shakra, bull of the Bharatas, the righteous, devoted to Vishnu and knower of truth, following the path?
Tell me this doubt as I ask, bull of the Bharatas: how was Vritra, tiger among kings, conquered by Shakra?
And how the battle was, tell me, grandsire, at length, mighty-armed; for my curiosity is great."
[Bhishma said:] "Long ago Indra went in a chariot with the hosts of gods and saw Vritra standing before him like a mountain.
Five hundred yojanas high, scourge of foes, and three hundred wide, and a little more.
Seeing that form, hard to conquer even for the three worlds, the gods were terrified and found no peace.
Then came to pass a battle fearful to the three worlds between Shakra, lord of the gods, and the great-souled Vritra.
With swords, battle-axes, spears, darts, clubs, rocks of many kinds and loud-sounding bows,
with various divine missiles and blazing meteors, the armies of gods and asuras made everything confused.
Led by the Grandfather, all the hosts of gods and the greatly fortunate sages came to see that battle.
Perfected beings came in the best aerial cars, great king, and gandharvas with apsarases in the best aerial cars.
Then Vritra, best of upholders of dharma, covering the sky, showered the lord of gods with a rain of rocks from the mountain.
Then the hosts of gods, angry, on every side with showers of weapons, turned aside the rain of rocks sent by Vritra in the battle.
Vritra, tiger of the Kurus, of great illusion and great strength, bewildered the lord of the gods on every side with a battle of illusion.
Shatakratu, afflicted by Vritra, fell into delusion; Vasishtha woke him there with the Rathantara.
[Vasishtha said:] "You are the best of gods, Devendra, destroyer of the gods' enemies, joined with the strength of the three worlds; why are you despondent, Shakra?
Here are Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, lords of the world, and the blessed god Soma, and all the great sages.
Do not be bewildered, Shakra, like some other man; making your mind noble in the battle, kill the enemy, lord of the gods.
The teacher of the world, three-eyed, saluted by all the worlds, the blessed one, looks at you; give up delusion, lord of the gods.
These Brahmarshis, led by Brihaspati, praise you for victory with divine praise, Shakra."
[Bhishma said:] As the great-souled Vasishtha thus roused him, the strength of Vasava, of supreme energy, grew greatly.
Then the blessed Pakashasana, regaining his understanding, joined with great yoga, drew away that illusion.
Then the glorious son of Angiras and those great sages, seeing Vritra's prowess, went to Maheshvara and said, for Vritra's destruction, wishing the good of the worlds:
Then the energy of the blessed lord of the world became a fever and entered the dreadful Vritra, best of Daityas.
And the blessed god Vishnu, honoured by all worlds, devoted to the protection of the worlds, entered Indra's thunderbolt.
Then the wise Brihaspati approached Shatakratu, with Vasishtha of great splendour and all the great sages.
Approaching Vasava, giver of boons, honoured by the worlds, with one-pointed minds they said, "Kill Vritra, lord."
[Maheshvara said:] "This Vritra, Shakra, is surrounded by great strength, the self of the universe, all-going, and renowned for his many illusions.
Kill that best of asuras, hard to conquer even for the three worlds, relying on yoga; do not despise him, lord of the gods.
By him austerity was performed for strength, lord of the immortals, for sixty thousand years, and Brahma gave him a boon.
Greatness of the yogis, great illusion, great strength, and foremost radiance, lord of the gods.
This is my energy entering Vritra, Vasava; do you too kill this Danava with the thunderbolt."
[Shakra said:] "Blessed one, by your grace I shall slay the son of Diti, so hard to approach, with the thunderbolt before your eyes, bull of the gods."
[Bhishma said:] When the Daitya, the great asura, was entered by fever, a great cry of joy arose from the gods and sages.
Then drums and conches of great sound, mridangas and dindimas were played by thousands.
A great loss of memory came upon all the asuras, and a mighty loss of knowledge in a moment.
Knowing him possessed, the sages and gods praised Shakra and urged on Ishana.
Shakra, the great-souled, standing in his chariot at the time of battle, praised by the sages, became of a form hard to look at.
His mouth blazed dreadfully, he became greatly pale, a great trembling of the limbs and a great panting seized him, and a fierce horripilation and a great sigh, king.
From his mouth issued a dreadful, inauspicious-seeming jackal-cry, a great horror, and its memory; blazing meteors fell burning at his side.
Vultures, herons and cranes uttered dreadful cries and, rejoicing, wheeled like a wheel over Vritra.
Then, mounting that chariot, strengthened by the gods in battle, Shakra with the thunderbolt raised in hand looked at the Daitya.
The great asura let out an inhuman cry and yawned, king of kings, joined with a fierce fever; and as he yawned, Shakra hurled the thunderbolt.
The thunderbolt of great splendour, like the fire of time, quickly felled the huge-bodied Daitya Vritra.
Then a great shout arose again on every side from the gods, Bharata, seeing Vritra slain.
Having slain Vritra, the blessed, greatly famous enemy of the Danavas entered heaven with the thunderbolt joined with Vishnu.
Skull-garlanded, lean, bloodied, Bharata, knower of dharma, clad in bark,
she came out, king of kings, in such a form, terrible, and then sought the wielder of the thunderbolt, best of the Bharatas.
After some time the slayer of Vritra, delight of the Kurus, went toward heaven, wishing the good of the worlds.
Seeing the mighty Shakra coming out of the lotus-stalk, she seized the lord of the gods by the neck, and clung well.
When that fear of Brahmin-slaying arose for him, he stayed hidden in the middle of a lotus-stalk in a lotus pond for many years.
Pursued with effort by that Brahmin-slaying, he was seized, Kauravya, and became motionless.
Shakra made the greatest effort to remove her, but the lord of the gods could not remove the Brahmin-slaying.
Seized by her, the lord of the gods, bull of the Bharatas, approached the Grandfather and honoured him with his head.
Knowing Shakra seized by the killing of a brahmana, Brahma then thought, best of the Bharatas.
The Grandfather, mighty-armed, spoke to the Brahmin-slaying, soothing her as it were, with a sweet voice, Bharata.
Let this lord of the thirty gods be released; do what pleases me, lady; say what I can do for you today, what wish you desire here.
[Brahmahatya said:] "The god honoured by the three worlds being pleased, the maker of the three worlds, I think it done; but ordain a dwelling for me.
This limit was made by you, wishing the protection of the worlds; a very great establishment was set by you, set in motion by the gods.
When you are pleased, knower of dharma, lord of all worlds, I shall depart from Shakra; ordain a dwelling for me."
[Bhishma said:] "So be it," the Grandfather then said to the Brahmin-slaying, and by a means he removed the Brahmin-slaying from Shakra.
Then Agni, meditated upon by the great-souled Self-born, approached Brahma and spoke.
I have come to you, blessed god, scourge of foes; what is to be done by me, god, you should tell.
[Brahma said:] "I shall divide this Brahmin-slaying in many ways for the release of Shakra today; take a fourth part of me."
[Agni said:] "What is the end of my release, Brahma? Think, lord; I wish to know this truly, honoured by the worlds."
[Brahma said:] "Whoever, a man in darkness, when you are blazing, does not sacrifice to you in the fire with seed, herb and juice,
the Brahmin-slaying will quickly go to him and dwell there itself; carrier of oblations, let the fever of your mind go."
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed, the eater of oblations and offerings to ancestors accepted that word of the Grandfather, and so it came to be, lord.
Then the Grandfather, calling together the trees, herbs and grasses, began to speak this matter, great king.
Then the trees, herbs and grass, being told as it was, trembled like fire, king, and said to Brahma:

Who else but us, grandfather of the world, for the Brahmin-slaying? Struck by our own nature, you should not strike us again.
mahabharata:12:273.37	We bear fire, cold, rain and wind constantly, god, and cutting and splitting.
mahabharata:12:273.38	This Brahmin-slaying today we shall take at your command, lord of the three worlds; think of our release.
[Brahma said:] "At the time of the joint, whoever through delusion cuts and splits, this will follow him."
[Bhishma said:] The trees, herbs and grass, thus addressed by the great soul, honoured Brahma and went quickly as they had come.
Then the Grandfather, calling the apsarases, spoke to them with sweet speech, soothing as it were, Bharata.
This Brahmin-slaying, fair ladies, has come from Indra; you are told: accept a fourth part of her.
[The apsarases said:] "For us whose minds are set on seizing, by your command, lord of the gods, think of our release, Grandfather."
[Brahma said:] "Whoever has union with women in their courses, her it will quickly go to; let the fever of your mind go."
[Bhishma said:] "So be it," said the groups of apsarases, glad-minded, and, reaching their places, they sported, bull of the Bharatas.
Then the maker of the three worlds, the great ascetic god, thought of the waters again; meditated on, they came.
All of them together came to Brahma of immeasurable splendour, and, bowing to the Grandfather, said these words, king.
We have come to you, god, scourge of foes; command us by your order, lord of the gods.
[Brahma said:] "This Brahmin-slaying, greatly fearful, came from Vritra to Indra; take a fourth part of her."
[The waters said:] "So be it, lord of the world, as you say, lord; you should think of our release."
You are the supreme teacher of all the world, lord of the gods; what other grace could raise us from this hardship?
[Brahma said:] "Thinking them small, a man bewildered in mind who releases phlegm, urine and excrement into you,
her it will quickly go to and dwell there itself; thus there will be release for you; I tell you the truth."
[Bhishma said:] Then, leaving the lord of the gods, the Brahmin-slaying, Yudhishthira, went to the place assigned by the gods' command.
Thus, lord of men, the Brahmin-slaying reached Shakra; having taken leave of the Grandfather, he arranged the horse sacrifice.
It is heard, great king, that the Brahmin-slaying that Vasava incurred was cleansed by the horse sacrifice.
Having regained fortune and slain thousands of foes, the god Vasava, lord of the earth, found incomparable delight.
From Vritra's blood, Partha, khukhundas were born; they are not to be eaten by the twice-born, nor by those initiated or rich in austerity.
In every state do what pleases these twice-born; for these are gods on earth, famed, delight of the Kurus.
Thus by Shakra of immeasurable splendour, Kauravya, through subtlety of mind, the great asura Vritra was slain by a means.
So you too, Kauravya, will be unconquered on earth, like the god Shatakratu, destroyer of foes.
Those who read this divine tale of Shakra on each festival day in the midst of brahmins will not incur sin.
Thus has the very wonderful great deed of Shakra concerning Vritra been told to you, dear; what more do you wish to hear?"
[Yudhishthira said:] "You said Vritra was bewildered by fever and slain by Vasava here with the thunderbolt, sinless one.
How did this fever arise, greatly wise one, and whence? I wish to hear the origin of fever in full, lord."
[Bhishma said:] "Hear, king, the world-famed origin of fever; I shall also tell its extent and kind, Bharata.
Long ago, great king, the peak of Meru, famed in the three worlds, called Jyotishka, belonging to Savitri, adorned with all jewels, immeasurable and unassailable in all worlds, Bharata,
there the god, on the mountain slope adorned with gold ores, sat shining like a couch.
The daughter of the king of mountains stood ever at his side, shining; so too the great-souled gods and the mighty Vasus.
Likewise the two great-souled Ashvins, best of physicians, and King Vaishravana, surrounded by guhyakas,
the glorious lord of the yakshas, dwelling at Kailasa, and Angiras and others, and other divine sages.
A pleasant, auspicious wind blew, carrying many scents, pure; great trees were in flower, endowed with the blossoms of all seasons.
Vidyadharas, perfected ones and ascetics attended Mahadeva, lord of beings, Bharata.
Beings too, great king, of many forms, and great fearful rakshasas and mighty pishachas,
of many shapes, delighted, raising various weapons, stood there as attendants of the god, like fire.
And the blessed Nandi stood there with the god's permission, holding a blazing trident, shining by its own splendour.
And Ganga, best of rivers, born of the waters of all holy places, attended that god in bodily form, delight of the Kurus.
Thus the blessed Mahadeva stayed there, honoured by gods, divine sages and the greatly fortunate gods.
After some time the Prajapati named Daksha, wishing to sacrifice by the rule told before, began.
Then all the gods, led by Shakra, assembled to go to his sacrifice and made up their minds.
Those great souls went in blazing aerial cars, shining like fire, by the god's leave, to Gangadvara, so it is heard.
Seeing the gods set out, the daughter of the king of mountains then spoke to the god Pashupati, her husband:
Blessed one, where are these gods, led by Shakra, going? Tell me truly, knower of truth; I have a great doubt.
[Maheshvara said:] "Daksha, fortunate one, the best lord of creatures, sacrifices with the horse sacrifice; the dwellers of heaven go there."
[Uma said:] "Why do you not go to this sacrifice, great one? By what prohibition does your going not occur?"
[Maheshvara said:] "This was all arranged by the gods themselves, fortunate one; in all sacrifices no share is assigned to me.
By the way that arose by the earlier means, fair one, the gods do not give me a share of the sacrifice by dharma."
[Uma said:] "Blessed one, in all beings you are superior in virtues in origin and power, unconquerable and unassailable in splendour, fame and fortune.
By this prohibition of your share, great one, a very great sorrow and trembling has arisen in me, sinless one."
[Bhishma said:] Having so spoken to the god Pashupati, her husband, the goddess became silent, king, with a burning mind.
Then, knowing the goddess's thought and what was in her heart that she wished, he commanded Nandin, "Stay."
Then, by the power of yoga, the lord of the lords of yoga, of great splendour, the god of gods, the bearer of the Pinaka, suddenly had that sacrifice destroyed by his terrible attendants.
Some let out cries, some laughed; others, king, scattered blood on the fire there.
Some tore up the sacrificial posts and wandered with deformed faces; others devoured the attendants with their mouths.
Then that sacrifice, king, being struck on every side, took the form of a deer and flew up into the sky.
Seeing the sacrifice so going, the lord took bow and arrow and followed it.
Then from the anger of that lord of the gods, of immeasurable splendour, a dreadful drop of sweat appeared, falling from his forehead.
As soon as that drop of sweat fell on the ground, a great fire like the fire of time arose.
In it a person was born then, bull among men, short, with exceedingly red eyes, green beard, terrifying.
With upright hair, hairy-limbed, like a hawk and an owl, fierce, dark in colour, clad in red.
That mighty being burnt the sacrifice like fire a dry patch, and all the gods, terrified, ran in the ten directions.
As that being moved about there, lord of the people, the earth, king, trembled greatly, bull of the Bharatas.
When cries of "Alas!" arose, a sound fearful to the worlds, the Grandfather spoke, showing himself to Mahadeva.

All the gods will give you a share too, lord; let withdrawal be made by you, lord of all the gods.
mahabharata:12:274.44	For all these gods and the sages, scourge of foes, have found no peace because of your anger, Mahadeva.
mahabharata:12:274.45	And this person, born of your sweat, best of the gods, will roam the worlds, knower of dharma, as the one called Fever.
Hearing this word of the king, those brahmanas, bull of the Bharatas, restrained and silent, went to Agni for refuge.
Brihaspati, do not in any way do for Marutta any rite, divine or ancestral, if you wish to please me.
And I wish to appease with your help the lord of the earth, with the great minister Sanjaya and the great chariot-warrior Kripa.

He set out, instructed by Keshava, mad with grief and tormented by the slaughter of his kin; but as he went in Keshava's presence, hastening, Babhru alone was suddenly slain by the great club released from a trick of a hunter, cursed by a Brahmana.
But Yudhishthira, wise, to the lord of the gods who had so spoken, said again these words, full of meaning:
Gain the worlds won by the Rajasuya and increased by the horse sacrifice, mighty-armed one, and the great fruit of your austerity.
